```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
library(SMSD)
term <- function(x, name) x$value[x$term == name]
fixed <- function(x, digits) formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")
```

## The Research Question

The standardized mean difference, δ = (μ<sub>1</sub> − μ<sub>2</sub>) / σ,
expresses the difference between two group means in standard deviation
units, so it is comparable across studies and measures. A common design
question is how many participants to collect in each group. When
participants are costly, and the two groups can have different costs per
participant, collecting more data buys a more accurate estimate of δ and
spends more of the budget.

Minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) balances the two. Chattopadhyay and
Kelley (2017) develop a purely sequential procedure that estimates δ
while minimizing a risk that combines squared estimation error with the
cost of sampling. The procedure assumes normal populations with a common
variance. It does not require that the variance or the effect size be
known in advance; the data collected so far say whether to stop.

## The Method

Write *d* for the sample standardized mean difference, the difference
between the two sample means divided by the pooled standard deviation
(Equations 2 and 3 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley, 2017). The risk prices
squared estimation error by a constant *A* and charges a cost *c* per
observation. With the large sample mean squared error of *d*, and group
sizes *n*<sub>1</sub> and *n*<sub>2</sub>, the approximate risk (their
Equation 9) is

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>A</i> {1 / <i>n</i><sub>1</sub> + 1 / <i>n</i><sub>2</sub> + &delta;<sup>2</sup> / (2 (<i>n</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>n</i><sub>2</sub>))} + <i>c</i> (<i>n</i><sub>1</sub> + <i>n</i><sub>2</sub>)</p>

With equal group sizes the risk is smallest at the optimal size per group
(their Equations 10 and 11)

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>n</i><sub><i>c</i></sub> = (<i>A</i> / (2 <i>c</i>))<sup>1/2</sup> &xi;, &nbsp; with &nbsp; &xi;<sup>2</sup> = 2 + &delta;<sup>2</sup> / 4</p>

where it equals 4 *c* *n*<sub>*c*</sub> (their Equation 12). Because δ,
and with it ξ, is unknown, the purely sequential rule estimates ξ from the
data, with *V*<sub>*n*</sub><sup>2</sup> = 2 + *d*<sup>2</sup> / 4 for the
*d* computed from *n* observations per group (their Equation 13), and
stops at the first *n* at or beyond the pilot sample size with (their
Equation 15)

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>n</i> &ge; (<i>A</i> / (2 <i>c</i>))<sup>1/2</sup> (<i>V</i><sub><i>n</i></sub> + <i>n</i><sup>&minus;&gamma;</sup>)</p>

The correction term *n*<sup>−γ</sup>, with γ a constant strictly between
0 and 1/2 (the article suggests 0.49, the default of the argument
`gamma`), keeps the rule from stopping too early. The pilot sample size
per group is the larger of a minimum *m*<sub>0</sub> and
(*A* / (2 *c*))<sup>1/(2 + 2γ)</sup>, rounded up (their Equation 14).

## The Sequential Workflow

`seq_mr_smd_pilot()` returns the pilot sample size, and `seq_mr_smd()`
evaluates the stopping rule on the data collected so far (at least four
observations per group, the smallest pilot sample size the article
allows). Its rows `next_n1` and `next_n2` give the size each group should
have at the next check. Neither function collects data or keeps state.
As with the other minimum risk procedures there is no confidence level:
the target is a risk, not a confidence interval.

Suppose a management researcher is estimating the effect of a new
onboarding program on employee engagement (measured on a standardized
scale) relative to the standard onboarding. Each participant costs the
same to recruit and measure, *c* = 5, and a unit of squared estimation
error is priced at *A* = 2,000. The article builds *A* as the amount one
would pay to have the estimate within a chosen distance of δ, divided by
the square of that distance; a team that would pay 500 for an estimate
within 0.5 has *A* = 500 / 0.5<sup>2</sup> = 2,000.

```{r pilot}
A       <- 2000   # price of one unit of squared estimation error
cost    <- 5      # cost per participant
pilot_n <- seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = A, c = cost)
pilot_n
```

To have data to work with, 60 engagement scores per group are simulated
here with a true standardized advantage of one half of a standard
deviation for the program group; they stand for the participants in the
order they would be recruited. The researcher collects the pilot sample
from each group and evaluates the rule.

```{r first-check}
set.seed(113)
program <- rnorm(60, mean = 0.5, sd = 1)
control <- rnorm(60, mean = 0.0, sd = 1)
check <- seq_mr_smd(program[1:pilot_n], control[1:pilot_n], A = A, c = cost)
check
```

At the pilot sample size the estimate rests on a handful of observations,
so it can be far from the true value. The rule is not met, and
recruitment continues one participant per group at a time (the sizes in
the rows `next_n1` and `next_n2`), with a new check after each pair. In a
study that is a call to `seq_mr_smd()` after each pair. With the scores
already in hand, `seq_path()` makes the same sequence of checks in one
call.

```{r path, fig.alt = "Current total sample size, a rising straight line, and criterion sample size, a nearly level stepped line, against the number of participants per group; the two first meet at the stopping point."}
path <- seq_path(seq_mr_smd, list(group_1 = program, group_2 = control),
                 A = A, c = cost)
attr(path, "stop_n")
plot(path, which = "criterion")
attr(path, "final_check")
```

```{r path-values, include = FALSE}
stop_n <- attr(path, "stop_n")
final <- attr(path, "final_check")
se_d <- sqrt((2 + 0.5^2 / 4) / stop_n)
```

The rule was first met at `r stop_n` participants per group, and that is
where the study ends. (The plot counts both groups together, as the check
does in its `Current n` and `Criterion n` lines.) The reported `smd` is
the minimum risk point estimate of δ. MRPE returns a point estimate and
no confidence interval, and at a sample this small the estimate is not
precise: the large sample standard error of *d* at `r stop_n` per group
is about `r fixed(se_d, 2)`, so an estimate of
`r fixed(term(final, "smd"), 2)` for a true value of 0.5 is
`r fixed(abs(term(final, "smd") - 0.5) / se_d, 1)` standard errors from
it. That is the accuracy these constants price, an estimate within about
0.5; a more accurate one takes a larger *A* relative to *c*.
`seq_report()` words the result for a methods section:

```{r report}
seq_report(path)
```

## Reproducing the Published Example

Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017, pp. 105 to 106) illustrate the procedure
with reading scores of children with high and low exposure to same
language subtitling. Assessing one child costs 2.40 dollars, and the team
would pay 2,500 dollars to estimate δ to within 0.5, so
*A* = 2,500 / 0.5<sup>2</sup> = 10,000. The pilot sample size is 13 per
group, and at the pilot data the estimate is 1.021484 and the rule is not
met, as in the article.

```{r published}
seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = 10000, c = 2.40)
high_sls <- c(11, 7, 22, 13, 6, 9, 11, 16, 12, 17, 14, 8, 16)
low_sls  <- c(3, 6, 10, 8, 14, 5, 12, 10, 6, 8, 13, 5, 9)
seq_mr_smd(high_sls, low_sls, A = 10000, c = 2.40)
```

The article then supposes that sampling continues and that *d* = 1.00
when *n* = 75 per group, where the rule is met for the first time. The
sibling package `DMAR` applies the same rule to summary statistics, which
shows the boundary:

```{r published-75}
attr(DMAR::mr_smd(d = 1.00, n = 74, A = 10000, sampling_cost = 2.40),
     "is_satisfied")
attr(DMAR::mr_smd(d = 1.00, n = 75, A = 10000, sampling_cost = 2.40),
     "is_satisfied")
```

With one cost and equal group sizes, `seq_mr_smd()` and `DMAR::mr_smd()`
give the same decision at every sample size; `seq_mr_smd()` works from
the raw data and also reports the criterion.

## Unequal Sampling Costs

When an observation costs more in one group than in the other, the best
design samples the less costly group more heavily. Chattopadhyay and
Kelley (2017) treat this case in the section "A General Scenario" (pp. 106
to 107, Equations 17 to 21, with the supporting Appendix B, Equations 41
to 43), and `seq_mr_smd()` implements that procedure when `c` is a vector
of two different costs, `c(c1, c2)`.

In the article's notation, and in the formulas of this section, subscript
1 marks the less costly group and subscript 2 the costlier one. (In the
argument `c = c(c1, c2)` the positions are group 1 and group 2, and either
group may be the costlier one.) The risk (their Equation 17) charges
*c*<sub>1</sub> *n*<sub>1</sub> + *c*<sub>2</sub> *n*<sub>2</sub> for
sampling. Setting its derivatives to zero (their Equation 41) shows that
the optimal sizes satisfy *n*<sub>2</sub>\* = *n*<sub>1</sub>\*
*r*(*n*<sub>1</sub>\*), with (their Equations 19 and 43)

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>r</i>(<i>n</i>) = {1 + (<i>c</i><sub>2</sub> &minus; <i>c</i><sub>1</sub>) <i>n</i><sup>2</sup> / <i>A</i>}<sup>&minus;1/2</sup></p>

and that *n*<sub>1</sub>\* solves

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>n</i><sub>1</sub>* = (<i>A</i> / <i>c</i><sub>1</sub>)<sup>1/2</sup> [1 + &delta;<sup>2</sup> / (2 {1 + <i>r</i>(<i>n</i><sub>1</sub>*)}<sup>2</sup>)]<sup>1/2</sup></p>

The sequential procedure starts from the pilot sample sizes of their
Equations 20 and 21, samples the less costly group one observation at a
time, keeps the costlier group at *n*<sub>1</sub> *r*(*n*<sub>1</sub>)
observations, rounded up, and stops at the first *n*<sub>1</sub> with

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>n</i><sub>1</sub> &ge; (<i>A</i> / <i>c</i><sub>1</sub>)<sup>1/2</sup> ([1 + <i>d</i><sup>2</sup> / (2 {1 + <i>r</i>(<i>n</i><sub>1</sub>)}<sup>2</sup>)]<sup>1/2</sup> + <i>n</i><sub>1</sub><sup>&minus;&gamma;</sup>)</p>

Suppose a participant in the control group costs twice as much to recruit
and measure as one in the program group, with costs of 4 and 8.

```{r unequal-pilot}
cost_2  <- c(4, 8)             # program, control
pilot_2 <- seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = A, c = cost_2)
pilot_2
```

The article's order is to add one participant to the less costly group,
bring the costlier group up to the size paired with it, and check. The
rows `next_n1` and `next_n2` of the result hold exactly those sizes, for
group 1 and group 2 as supplied, so the loop only has to bring each group
up to its row. It runs unchanged whichever group is the costlier one;
pairing the sizes the other way around would oversample. The two groups
grow at different rates, so this is a loop that `seq_path()`, which takes
the same number of observations from each group at every stage, does not
replace. The scores are those simulated above, taken in the order the
participants would be recruited, so the two designs can be compared on
the same people.

```{r unequal-loop}
n <- unname(pilot_2)           # group sizes at the first check
repeat {
  check <- seq_mr_smd(program[1:n[1]], control[1:n[2]], A = A, c = cost_2)
  if (attr(check, "is_satisfied")) break
  n <- check$value[check$term %in% c("next_n1", "next_n2")]
}
check
```

```{r unequal-values, include = FALSE}
n_2 <- c(term(check, "current_n1"), term(check, "current_n2"))
se_d_2 <- sqrt(1 / n_2[1] + 1 / n_2[2] + 0.5^2 / (2 * sum(n_2)))
```

The less costly program group ends with more participants than the
control group, `r n_2[1]` against `r n_2[2]`, where the single cost of
`r cost` ended with `r stop_n` in each. The rule is decided group by
group: `optimal_n1` and `optimal_n2` are each group's own criterion, and
the rule is met when each group has reached its own. Once it is met,
`next_n1` and `next_n2` equal the current sizes: nothing more is called
for. The estimate, `r fixed(term(check, "smd"), 2)`, is
`r fixed(abs(term(check, "smd") - 0.5) / se_d_2, 1)` standard errors from
the true 0.5 (the large sample standard error at these sizes is about
`r fixed(se_d_2, 2)`): again a point estimate from a small sample, as
accurate as these constants price it and no more.

Three points about the two cost procedure matter to anyone comparing the
package with the article.

1. Equations 18 and 42 of the article, and the stopping rule built on
   them, are printed with {1 + *r*(*n*<sub>1</sub>)} to the first power.
   The derivatives in Equation 41 give the second power shown above; only
   the second power minimizes the risk in Equation 17, and only it reduces
   to Equation 10 when the costs are equal. `seq_mr_smd()` uses the second
   power. For *A* = 50,000, costs of 2 and 8, and δ = 1, the printed form
   gives an optimal *n*<sub>1</sub> of 183.4, while direct minimization of
   the risk gives 175.7 (both figures are in the Details of
   `?seq_mr_smd`).
2. The article's two cost procedure does not reduce to its one cost
   procedure when the costs are equal: its pilot uses *A* / *c*<sub>1</sub>
   where Equation 14 uses *A* / (2 *c*), and its correction term is
   (*A* / *c*<sub>1</sub>)<sup>1/2</sup> *n*<sup>−γ</sup> where Equation 15
   has (*A* / (2 *c*))<sup>1/2</sup> *n*<sup>−γ</sup>. `seq_mr_smd()` uses
   the one cost procedure whenever the two costs supplied are equal, and
   the two cost procedure whenever they differ. Two costs that differ only
   by rounding error (a relative difference of at most
   `sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)`, which is
   `r format(signif(sqrt(.Machine$double.eps), 2))`, as between `24 * 0.1`
   and `2.4`) count as equal.
3. The article assumes that the first group is the less costly one.
   `seq_mr_smd()` accepts the costs in either order.

## What to Expect Before the Study

`seq_mr_smd_sensitivity()` runs the whole procedure many times on
simulated data with a known δ and compares the result with the best fixed
sample size. It answers, before any data are collected, how many
participants a choice of *A* and *c* implies and how close the procedure
comes to the minimum risk.

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- seq_mr_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, A = A, c = cost, G = 500,
                               seed = 2017)
sens
```

`optimal_n1` and `optimal_n2` are the fixed sample sizes that minimize
the risk if δ were known, and `minimum_risk` is the risk there. The mean
final sample size is above the optimum, about
`r fixed(term(sens, "mean_n1"), 0)` per group against
`r fixed(term(sens, "optimal_n1"), 0)` (`ratio_n1`), which is the price of
the correction term at a sample this small, and the realized risk is
close to the minimum (`risk_efficiency`, to be read against its Monte
Carlo standard error, `se_risk_efficiency`). The guarantees are
asymptotic: both ratios approach 1 as *A* / *c* grows. With the article's
own settings the package reproduces its Tables 1 and 3 within Monte Carlo
error, as the Details of `?seq_mr_smd` report; for example, for
*A* = 50,000, *c* = 1, and δ = 0 the mean final sample size per group in
5,000 replications was 235.04 against an optimum of
`r fixed(sqrt(50000 / 2) * sqrt(2), 1)`, and Table 1 of the article
(p. 103) reports 235.04.

The same function accepts two costs, a batch size (`batch`, the number of
observations added between checks), and a skewed population
(`distribution = "skewed"`), which shows what a violation of the
normality assumption costs.

## Relationship to Accuracy in Parameter Estimation

When the design goal is a confidence interval for δ of a target width,
and not the minimum of a loss that combines cost and error, use the
accuracy in parameter estimation procedure `seq_aipe_smd()` (Kelley,
Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018; Kelley & Rausch, 2006; Maxwell, Kelley, &
Rausch, 2008). In `DMAR`, the fixed sample size counterpart
`ss_aipe_smd()` plans the sample size when a value of δ can be supposed
in advance.
